name: Lagoon
notes: Sheltered coastal lagoons: mangroves and sea purslane on tropical lagoon shores, samphire/saltwort and reeds on temperate barrier lagoons (Venice, Baltic haffs), and dense seagrass meadows in the shallow water. Drawn on Caribbean and Indo-Pacific atoll lagoons, Mediterranean and Baltic lagoons; underwater species flagged.

growth.juvenile_note: Viviparous: the seed sprouts on the tree and a green, pencil-like hypocotyl 20-30 cm long hangs from the brown fruit. It drops, floats (weeks, up to a year), lodges upright in mud, roots from the lower tip within days and opens a pair of glossy leaves at the top. The sapling is a single stem that soon throws down arching red-brown prop roots.
growth.source: Tropical Plants Database (theferns.info) Rhizophora mangle (1-1.5 m/yr on productive sites; 5-20 m, rarely 30; flowers year-round; flowering by 6 yr, even 3-5 yr at 0.5-1 m tall; propagules 8-30 cm); Wikipedia (to 24 m, commonly ~6 m; propagules may float over a year); lifespan and shade estimated

fruiting.source: Tropical Plants Database (flowers all year; bees and wind; 4-7 months from fertilization to hypocotyl emergence plus 4-6 months more before it falls; propagules 8-30 cm); Wikipedia (pale yellow flowers; self or wind pollination); fruit size given for the hanging propagule; set, crop and decay estimated

canopy.name: Coconut palm

growth.juvenile_note: The husked nut lies on the sand and after 2-6 months a pointed shoot pushes out of one end while the nut's flesh feeds the seedling. First leaves are entire, stiff, strap-like blades split only at the tip (bifid), in a stemless fan-like rosette; pinnate fronds come later, and a trunk rises after ~3-5 years, widening from a bulbous base ('bole').
growth.source: Wikipedia Coconut (tall palms bear at 6-10 yr, live 60-100 yr; ~11 months from female flower opening to harvest; up to 15 inflorescences/yr; ~80 nuts/yr, up to 150; nut ~1.4 kg; largely cross-pollinated, dwarfs selfing); ICRAF Agroforestree (tall selections 24-30 m, flowers after ~6th yr); germination from FAO coconut guides

canopy.source: Palm of tropical coasts worldwide; height 15-30 m. Leaning trunk, feather crown; sea-dispersed nuts. Standard floras and Kew POWO for the name.

canopy.name: Sea hibiscus

growth.juvenile_note: The hairy capsules split and the seeds, which float for months, come up on the strand line as a stem with round, heart-shaped, grey-backed leaves. The young plant branches low and grows fast; its long limbs bend down, touch the ground and root, so a single tree soon becomes a low, tangled, impenetrable thicket on the lagoon shore.
growth.source: Elevitch & Thomson 2006 Species Profiles for Pacific Island Agroforestry, Hibiscus tiliaceus (tree 4-10 m, rarely 15; fast-growing; flowers in 2-3 years; seeds and capsules float; low branches layer to form thickets); timings estimated.

repro.note: each flower lasts one day, yellow in the morning and orange-red by evening; long limbs root where they touch the ground

canopy.source: Talipariti tiliaceum (basionym Hibiscus tiliaceus), sea hibiscus or beach hibiscus: sprawling coastal tree 4-10 m of lagoon shores, beach crests and mangrove landward edges throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific, also on Caribbean coasts — Elevitch & Thomson 2006; Flora of China vol. 12. Kew POWO accepted name Talipariti tiliaceum.

fruit.form: small hairy ovoid capsules about 2 cm splitting into five

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two small green cotyledons, then a thread-like stem bearing whorls of tiny toothed scale leaves on jointed green twigs, like a horsetail. Grows 1-3 m a year as a narrow pine-like cone with a straight leader and drooping needle-like branchlets, only later opening into an irregular wispy crown.
growth.source: PROSEA (early growth >3 m/yr, >10 m at 10 yr, lifespan 40-50 yr, epigeal germination within 2 weeks, no pretreatment, seedlings fail in the shade of Casuarina stands); Parrotta 1993 USDA SO-ITF-SM-46 (flowering from 2-3 yr)

fruiting.source: PROSEA Casuarina equisetifolia (male spikes 7-40 mm at twig tips, female heads grow into woody cone-like infructescences 10-24 x 9-13 mm, wind-pollinated, cones mature 18-20 weeks after flowering, valves open to release samaras 6-8 mm); Parrotta 1993 (two flowering peaks)

The seedling shows two small cotyledons, then opposite, bright yellow-green, fleshy, club-shaped leaves 1-2 cm long on a few pale stems; the stems then sprawl and root at the nodes, knitting a low, dense, succulent carpet.

growth.juvenile_note: The tiny corky two-winged fruits float on the tide and sprout on wet sand or marl above the mangroves. Seedlings carry small leathery lance-shaped leaves (silvery-hairy in the silver form) and soon branch from the base into a bushy, often leaning, multi-stemmed shrub that ages into a gnarled, twisted small tree; broken branches root readily.
growth.source: Useful Tropical Plants (theferns.info: 4-20 m, medium growth, full sun, sow fresh seed, large cuttings root); Wikipedia (multi-trunked shrub 1-4 m to tree 20 m); FNPS (long-lived, flowers/fruits all year); ResearchGate buttonwood germination study (germination peaking in week 2)

It hardens into a woody-based, densely branched evergreen bush of glaucous succulent leaves, often forming low hummocks on shingle at the top of salt marshes; leaves may redden in winter.
growth.source: Wikipedia Suaeda vera (small shrub of arid salt flats and salt marshes; in Britain mainly where shingle meets salt marsh; seeds germinate more readily in fresh than in salt water). Stature (to ~1.2 m), growth rate, age at first flowering and lifespan estimated from shrubby halophytes.

fruiting.source: British flora accounts (tiny green petal-less flowers 1-3 in the leaf axils, Jul-Oct; fruit a utricle in the persistent fleshy perianth with one shiny black seed ~1-1.5 mm). Pollination, ripening, persistence and crop estimated from Suaeda biology.

bark.note: submerged; short vertical shoots from a buried rhizome

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds about 1 cm long are released when the ripe fruit splits and root within days on the sandy bottom. The seedling is a short shoot of 2-5 flat, bright-green ribbon leaves with rounded tips, anchored by a few thick roots; it grows a buried rhizome and after a year or two starts sending up new leaf shoots, spreading into a patch.
growth.source: Wikipedia Thalassia testudinum (leaves to 30 cm x 2 cm; rhizomes 5-10 cm deep; flowers Apr-Jul; fruit 20-25 mm with 1-6 seeds, splitting after ~8 weeks; low-tide mark to 30 m). Seed germination without dormancy, shoot lifespan (up to ~10-15 yr by leaf-scar ageing) and seedling-to-flowering time estimated from seagrass literature.

ground.name: Manatee grass

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are rare; new shoots come mostly from the creeping rhizome. Each short shoot carries two or three round, spaghetti-thin, bright-green leaves that grow to 30 cm or more and sway with the current; shoots spaced along the rhizome make a loose meadow, often mixed with turtle grass.
growth.source: Littler & Littler / Smithsonian Marine Station (Syringodium filiforme: terete leaves 1-2 mm thick, to 30-50 cm, 2-4 per shoot; subtidal to ~20 m; flowering uncommon); timings estimated.

repro.note: dioecious; pollen carried underwater; spreads mostly by rhizomes

ground.source: Syringodium filiforme, manatee grass: seagrass with round spaghetti-thin leaves, shallow lagoons and back-reef flats of the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico and Florida, 10-50 cm — Smithsonian Marine Station at Fort Pierce species account; Kew POWO for the name (underwater).

ground.name: Shoal grass

growth.juvenile_note: A new shoot is a tuft of two to four flat, very narrow, pale-green leaves with a notched, three-toothed tip, rising from a thin rhizome in shallow sand. It spreads fast along the rhizome and is the first seagrass to colonise bare lagoon shallows, forming a short, fine meadow that can stand exposure at the lowest tides.
growth.source: Smithsonian Marine Station at Fort Pierce (Halodule wrightii: flat leaves 1-3 mm wide, 5-20 cm or more, tip 2-3-toothed; pioneer species of shallow and intertidal flats, tolerant of exposure and salinity swings); timings estimated.

repro.note: dioecious; pollen carried underwater; buried seeds form a seed bank; spreads fast by rhizomes

ground.source: Halodule wrightii, shoal grass: fine flat-leaved pioneer seagrass of the shallowest lagoon flats, Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the Americas and the Caribbean, 5-25 cm — Smithsonian Marine Station at Fort Pierce species account; Kew POWO for the name (underwater).

ground.name: Seashore paspalum

growth.juvenile_note: Seed is set sparingly and most new plants are rooted runner tips. A young plant is a small tuft of flat, two-ranked, dark green blades; long stolons and rhizomes then creep over wet sand and mud, rooting at the nodes, and turn it into a dense, bright-green turf with paired, finger-like flower spikes standing just above the leaves.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 25 (Paspalum vaginatum: rhizomatous and stoloniferous perennial, culms 10-79 cm, blades 2-15 cm x 2-8 mm, racemes usually 2, paired; brackish shores, tidal flats and ditches); timings estimated.
